t: Delete Columns to Make Sorted II — Greedy Column-by-Column
o:
We must delete the fewest columns so that the remaining strings, read left to right, are in non-decreasing lexicographic order. The key observation is that we process columns greedily from left to right: a column is kept if and only if keeping it does not break order among rows that are still 'tied' (equal on all previously kept columns). Rows already strictly ordered by earlier columns are unaffected by any later column, so only ties matter.

**Example 1** `strs = ["ca","bb","ac"]`: column 0 gives c > b < a — not sorted. If we keep it, no choice of later columns can fix 'ca' vs 'ac' (c... vs a...), so we must delete column 0. Then column 1 gives a <= b <= c: sorted with 1 deletion.

**Example 2** `strs = ["xc","yb","za"]`: column 0 gives x < y < z, so every row pair is already strictly ordered; column 1 can never break anything. Answer 0.

**Example 3** `["zyx","wvu","tsr"]`: every column is non-increasing top to bottom, so each must be deleted; answer 3.

With n, W ≤ 100, an O(n·W) or O(n·W·W) scan is trivially fast, so correctness of the greedy matters more than micro-optimization.
k: Process columns left to right; keep a column iff it doesn't violate order among rows that are currently tied.
Once two adjacent rows are strictly ordered by some kept prefix of columns, later columns cannot break that pair.
Track per-row-pair state (ordered / tied) incrementally instead of re-comparing full prefixes.

a.i: Try every subset of columns to delete (or equivalently keep) and check whether the resulting strings are sorted. This directly mirrors the problem definition and establishes a baseline. It's exponential but fine conceptually since constraints are tiny.
s: Enumerate all subsets S of kept columns (2^W subsets).
For each subset, build the projected strings using columns in S.
Check whether the projected array is non-decreasing.
Return the minimum W - |S| over valid subsets.
a.t: O(2^W · n · W) — enumerating subsets and checking each projection.
a.sp: O(n · W) for the projected strings.

a.i: Scan columns left to right, maintaining for each row whether it is already strictly greater than the previous row based on kept columns so far ('cut'). When examining a new column: if any still-tied adjacent pair would be violated (prev char > cur char), delete this column; otherwise keep it and mark pairs as cut where prev char < cur char. This greedy is optimal because deleting a column only helps future columns, so whenever a conflict forces a deletion now, deferring it cannot reduce total deletions.
s: Initialize a boolean array cut where cut[i] means row i is already strictly after row i-1.
For each column c, check all adjacent pairs i where !cut[i]: if strs[i][c] > strs[i+1][c], mark the column for deletion and skip it.
If the column survives, set cut[i] = true for every tied pair with strs[i][c] < strs[i+1][c].
Count and return the number of deleted columns.
a.t: O(n · W) — each column is scanned at most twice over all rows.

w: In an interview, go straight to the greedy after stating the tie-tracking insight; mention brute force only briefly to show you considered alternatives. Common pitfalls: comparing full strings each time instead of tracking which pairs are already ordered (still correct but slower), forgetting that equal characters leave a pair tied, and assuming column-wise sortedness alone suffices (it doesn't — Example 2 shows rows need not be internally sorted). Edge cases: single string (answer 0), single character columns, all identical strings (delete nothing needed? actually all-tied forever → delete violating columns only; identical rows are always fine). Follow-ups: prove greedy optimality via exchange argument, or handle streaming columns where deletions must be decided online (the same greedy works since it never revisits earlier decisions).
